title: Cell-free identification of de novo designed minibinders as building blocks for targeted protein degraders
summary: Targeted protein degradation is a powerful strategy for manipulating protein abundance and function, but developing protein-based degraders typically requires laborious screening and optimization of target-specific binders. Recent advances in de novo protein design offer a promising route to accelerate degrader development, although computationally designed binders often exhibit variable binding activity and require extensive experimental validation. Here, we developed a rapid screening platform that couples cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) with enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) to identify functional miniprotein binders directly from computational designs. Using β-catenin as a model target, we screened 93 de novo designed minibinders for expression and binding activity in less than three days, identifying six candidates with half-maximal effective concentrations below 500 nM. Two lead minibinders exhibited binding affinities of 299 and 335 nM and, without further affinity maturation, were fused to an engineered E3 ubiquitin ligase to generate functional protein degraders. These constructs reduced cytosolic β-catenin levels by approximately 80% and 60%, respectively, and suppressed β-catenin-dependent transcriptional activity in mammalian cells. These findings demonstrate that moderate-affinity, computationally designed minibinders can support effective targeted protein degradation without iterative binder optimization. More broadly, our integrated design and screening workflow provides a rapid and accessible approach for converting de novo protein binders into functional intracellular degraders.
